#122083. Latest Update: Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (828 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want to price more precisely?
  • It has been revealed that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers noted no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

It has been revealed that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer remarked yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

According to recent reports, imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Industry observers note that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

Recent findings suggest that it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Industry observers note that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

According to recent reports, “I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Industry observers note that find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Industry observers note that sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

It has been revealed that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Industry observers note that roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Darryl Davis Seminars Inc.’s multi-million dollar federal trademark infringement lawsuit against Epique Realty, which accuses the virtual brokerage of unlawfully using the POWER AGENT® brand in its nationwide operations, is headed to court next week.

It has been revealed that during the first week of December, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Upcoming York will hold a hearing on a motion for a preliminary injunction filed by Darryl Davis and his firm that would bar Epique Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, from using the POWER AGENT trademark.

Originally filed in late June, the lawsuit alleges that Houston-based Epique Realty adopted the POWER AGENT name and “built an entire brand architecture around it” despite being put on notice and asked to stop, according to the announcement. In addition to Epique Realty, the lawsuit also lists Joshua Miller, Janice Delcid, Christopher Miller, XYZ Corps 1-10 and John and Jane Does 1-10 as defendants.

Darryl Davis Seminars indicates it has used the POWER AGENT mark continuously since 1993 through The POWER Program, which it describes as the real estate industry’s oldest and longest-running agent training and coaching platform.

“POWER AGENT® has been our name since 1993, and both it and THE POWER PROGRAM® are registered trademarks,” Davis told HousingWire. “The law expects a trademark owner to protect its marks. We have for decades, and we will keep doing so. Because the matter is pending, I will let our court filings speak to the rest.”.

In a recent development, in October, Epique filed a counterclaim asking for a ruling from the court that Davis’s trademark registrations of Power Agent programs do not give his firm exclusive rights to the word “power” and that this does not give Davis or his organization the rights to a family of “Power” trademarks. Epique is also asking the court to force Davis and his firm to prove likely confusing for each expression of “Power” Epique was accused of. Epique is also seeking rulings from the court that its current uses of PowerFlex and PowerCon, do not infringe on Davis’s trademarks and that it is not liable “merely because an independently controlled agent or third party used POWER-formative wording.”.

Sources indicate that epique emphasized in the filing that its agents are independent contractors and that the firm does not hold passwords for agents’ personal social media accounts in order to edit or delete content, nor does it review agents’ social media posts or websites before they are published. This contradicts Davis’s complaint, which alleges that the brokerage’s independent contractor agreement requires agents to submit marketing or advertising posts for approval prior to publication. Additionally, the company said that under state law in Texas, where Epique is headquartered, the firm is only responsible for ensuring that advertising content produced by agents complies with state rules.

In a filing earlier this month, Davis largely denied Epique’s counterclaims, namely that he is trying to trademark the word “Power” by itself and he and his firm rejected Epique’s request that the court declares that Darryl Davis Seminars does not own the word “power” exclusively and that it does not have an across-the-board monopoly over trademarks containing the word. Throughout the filing, Davis maintained that Epique infringed on his firm’s trademarks and he asked the court to reject Epique’s counter claims.

It has been revealed that this news was first reported by Inman. Epique Realty did not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

Previously, another two wallets linked to the Ethereum Foundation transferred 4,393 ETH ($11.1 million at that time) to the Kraken exchange on October 12.

In a recent development, this transactions are not impulsive moves but part of a carefully planned 10-year strategy. Over the past decade, a total of 49,751 ETH has been sent from these addresses to exchanges.

The average selling price was a modest $658 by today's standards, although it’s worth noting that these coins were originally acquired in the project's early days, when ETH was worth less than a dollar.

According to recent reports, ethereum is at the moment going through one of its most challenging times in recent memory. Investor sentiment is still low, network activity has dispersed throughout Layer-2 solutions.

In addition to that, Ethereum has spent most of 2026 underperforming many rival ecosystems.

Earlier this year, Hsiao-Wei Wang has stepped down from the roles of co-executive director and board member of the Ethereum Foundation. In February, fellow co-Executive Director Tomasz Stańczak also stepped down.

Industry observers note that ethereum foundation has been selling ETH in 2026 during steep price movements, both up and down. For instance, BitMine acquired 10,000 ETH at an average price of $2,292 this June.

A similar sale one week earlier, where another 10,000 ETH was sold at $2,387 per coin.

Sources indicate that on Friday, Bitcoin price dropped below $60,000. At some point, it fell 5.10% to $55,830, the lowest level since September 2024.

It has been revealed that liquidations on crypto exchanges reached $1.57 billion over 24 hours on Nov. 20. According to CoinGlass, 265,525 traders were liquidated over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of the total.

Bitcoin saw $554.28 million in liquidations, and 91.3% of that amount came from long positions.

Ethereum fell below $1,700 on Nov. 20, and ETH traders saw $331.08 million in liquidations.

Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.
  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • Industry observers note that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

Industry observers note that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA stated.

In a recent development, in its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the manufacturer looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Newly introduced Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn debuts reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA remarked.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA mentioned it will share more as the investigation continues.

Tech Report: Voice AI startup ElevenLabs reportedly seeking fresh funding at $33B valuation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc.
  • According to recent reports, bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the company intends to close the round in the first quarter of 2027.
  • It’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:42 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc. is reportedly in early talks to raise capital at a $33 billion valuation.

According to recent reports, bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the company intends to close the round in the first quarter of 2027. According to the report, some investors are pushing for the raise to happen sooner. That hints the planned round may include a secondary sale, a transaction that enables existing investors to cash out their shares.

It’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom. Late-stage startup investments almost always include contributions from existing backers. ElevenLabs’ most recent raise, which valued it at $22 billion, saw the participation of Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund, Blackrock, Wellington and several others.

Industry observers note that elevenLabs’ fundraising push reportedly comes amid a surge in customer demand. Its annualized revenue is said to have grown by $100 million since September, to $700 million.

Founded in 2022, ElevenLabs develops a series of AI models optimized to process audio. Companies use them to field call center inquiries, transcribe meetings, generate music and perform related tasks. It also offers a service called Productions that delivers ready-to-use audio assets.

According to recent reports, the company debuted its newest and most capable model, Eleven v4, in late September. The algorithm’s flagship feature is its ability to tailor its speaking style to each text snippet. It does so by automatically tuning parameters such as tone and pacing.

In a recent development, owners can manually customize Eleven v4’s speaking style by adding instructions to scripts. They can also generate conversations with multiple synthetic speakers. A real-time version of the model, Eleven v4 Turbo, generates audio with only 150 milliseconds of latency for use cases such as customer support.

ElevenLabs offers Eleven v4 alongside more narrowly focused models. In May, it introduced an algorithm specifically optimized to dub videos. Additionally, it provides developer tools that make it easier to integrate its AI models into enterprise applications.

It’s possible ElevenLabs is raising new capital to finance more acquisitions. Earlier this month, it agreed to buy Kotoba Inc., a startup that develops audio processing models for companies in Japan. Nikkei Asia reported that the deal is worth $100 million. ElevenLabs will hire more salespeople in Japan over the next few months to grow its market presence.

A few days before the acquisition, ElevenLabs chief executive Mati Staniszewski stated that the manufacturer plans to start preparing for an initial public offering in 2028. That time frame suggests the round the software maker is presently raising could be followed by additional venture investments.

Latest Update: Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon mentioned in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

It has been revealed that the terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

Industry observers note that “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan stated in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

In a recent development, inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s vital to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

In a recent development, tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

Industry observers note that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really key component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

#122076. BOXABL financial filing highlights cash burn and scaling risk

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2306 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

BOXABL financial filing highlights cash burn and scaling risk

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: HousingWire TBD author Dan Oppenheim contributed financial analysis and insight for this report.].
  • Factory-built housing’s promise of a not-so-distant brighter future has always been compelling.
  • It has been revealed that forever, it seems, it has carried an “always within five years” sense of inevitability, stuck in limbo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: HousingWire TBD author Dan Oppenheim contributed financial analysis and insight for this report.].

Factory-built housing’s promise of a not-so-distant brighter future has always been compelling.

It has been revealed that forever, it seems, it has carried an “always within five years” sense of inevitability, stuck in limbo. Build homes faster, with less waste, fewer labor constraints, greater consistency, in conditioned indoor offsite space, and at costs low enough to bend asking-price curves toward households priced out of homeownership.

Industry observers note that the arrival of housing’s future, however, seems caught in the unforgiving calculus of time and space’s infinite divisibility. Progress happens and promises soar, but the ultimate goal of powering United States home development and construction with modern manufacturing going concerns keeps falling short, trapped in an echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet.

In a recent development, the rub has always been turning the promise of housing’s future into a business that can reliably produce homes, deliver them to customers, cover its costs, and generate enough cash to keep doing it. Many homebuilding business leaders who’ve tried a lot of things and kept doing what works are apt to think of all that as homebuilding’s never-ending siren’s song, one that, should it emerge, should be dispelled as a wishful-thinking distraction.

BOXABL, the Las Vegas-based modular housing manufacturer that completed its Nasdaq listing in July, now faces that test amid mounting difficulties, including self-inflicted ones.

Its November 16, 2026, quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission provides data to address questions that experienced homebuilding executives have long raised about factory-based housing ventures and that they have expressed about BOXABLE.

It has been revealed that can a manufacturer achieve sufficient production volume to absorb fixed costs? Can it coordinate factory output with site readiness, permitting, installation, and customer financing? And can it sustain those operations when capital is expensive, construction inputs remain inflation-pressured, and affordability-constrained homebuyers are wavering for any of half a dozen good reasons?

BOXABL’s filing shows progress in generating orders. It also shows that the organization’s operating model still falls far short of demonstrating the economic soundness, scalability, and durability required to sustain a residential construction business. The company’s options have not disappeared, but they have narrowed, and time is swiftly passing. Management has less room and less time to demonstrate the business’s financial sustainability.

BOXABL’s Form 10-Q, filed on November 16 for the quarter ended September 30, reports $14 million in unrestricted cash, down from $29 million at year-end 2025. During the most recent quarter, the company used $6 million in cash for operations, down from $8.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. This translates to a cash burn rate of about $2 million per month, so the $14 million of unrestricted cash on hand as of the end of Q3 represents seven months of operations.

It has been revealed that that metric doesn’t precisely forecast when BOXABL might run out of cash. Instead, it shows the relationship between available resources and BOXABL’s most recent cash-burn rate.

In Note 4 of the filing, the company states: “Substantial doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern exists.”.

Is the disclosure a prediction of failure? Technically and officially, no. Management identifies continued cost controls, accelerated Casita deliveries and sales, and additional equity financing as measures intended to address the uncertainty. There’s no ambiguity that those measures must deliver results even as the tech giant continues to consume cash.

In a recent development, BOXABL reported 209 net orders for Casitas in Q3, bringing its total for the first nine months to 362 net orders. As of September 30, the tech giant had 679 Casitas in backlog, representing approximately $45 million in potential revenue. Those figures indicate customer interest but raise what are arguably the most important questions for BOXABL – how legitimate the orders are, how much of the backlog will convert to revenue, and when that conversion will occur.

The point is that while most homebuilders count a signed contract as an order only after the customer has satisfied mortgage qualification, BOXABL notes that 85 Casitas in the backlog (and recorded as an order during a recent quarter) are pending feasibility studies to assess whether the customer’s site can support installation.

In addition, another 311 units in the backlog were associated with orders that were one to two years old, raising questions about whether they will convert to revenue. Together, these 396 units, the 85 units that still require feasibility assessment, and the 311 older orders represent 58% of the tech giant’s reported backlog of 679 units.

Industry observers note that that disconnect is not merely a scheduling matter. Backlog becomes financially meaningful only when orders reliably convert to completed sales. For BOXABL, that conversion process remains insufficiently demonstrated, likely raising investor doubts about the authenticity of the orders and the cleanliness of the backlog.

Sources indicate that during the first nine months of 2026, BOXABL generated $2.629 million in revenue, up from $588,000 a year earlier. It delivered 36 Casitas, compared with eight in the prior-year period. However, cost of goods sold totaled $13.78 million, resulting in a gross loss of $11.15 million.

It has been revealed that approximately $10 million of those costs were inventory valuation adjustments and allowances for slow-moving or obsolete inventory. These accounting charges should not be mistaken for the direct manufacturing cost of the 36 delivered units. Nevertheless, they reflect the economic consequences of producing and carrying inventory that would not generate sufficient revenue.

Looking at BOXABL’s production costs, excluding obsolete inventory, inventory adjustments, scrapped inventory, warranty expense, and allocations such as stock-based compensation expense, the tech giant reported a cost of Casitas sold of $2.075 million for the first nine months of the year, compared with $2.629 million in revenue, leaving an adjusted gross profit of approximately $550,000.

Recent findings suggest that however, when assessing BOXABL’s ability to produce Casitas at a profit, it’s difficult to ignore the message and significance of the largest component of the inventory charge, $7.4 million, which represented an adjustment to reduce the carrying value of the inventory to its realizable value. Although that charge affects more inventory than was sold in the first nine months of 2026, it is unclear whether BOXABL’s newly produced inventory would sell at or above its cost of production.

BOXABL is not presently scaled – from a management perspective – for this low level of volume and revenue. Its $2.629 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026 was dwarfed by $15.553 million in operating expenses, which included general and administrative expenses, sales and marketing, and research and development. BOXABL has developed a product and a manufacturing system.

By any measure, however, its reported results have not yet demonstrated that the system can operate at volumes and margins sufficient to sustain it.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most revealing figures concern inventory. At September 30, BOXABL reported $17.645 million in inventory for 388 units, including 198 finished Casitas and 190 work-in-process units. While this inventory balance may not sound like much, it represents 6.7x the revenue generated during the first nine months of 2026. That $17.645 million of inventory is also after adjustments (write-downs), as the cost to produce the inventory was $10 million higher.

According to recent reports, management explains that significant finished inventory remains on hand because customer sites are not ready for delivery and installation. Delays stem from feasibility studies, permitting, land preparation, and other deployment requirements. That disclosure addresses a problem that residential construction executives understand.

Manufacturing a housing unit is only one part of delivering a completed home. Factory efficiencies cannot eliminate the complexities of land preparation, local regulations, logistics, installation, and customer financing.

According to recent reports, when manufacturing and delivery schedules diverge, capital remains tied up in products that cannot yet generate revenue. Inventory must be stored, managed, and sometimes modified to meet changing specifications. BOXABL’s filing reports that approximately $7.1 million of finished goods was reclassified as work in process in 2025 to accommodate modifications for California’s modular housing requirements.

None of this establishes that the manufacturing approach cannot work. It demonstrates that the economic benefits of industrialized construction must be measured across the entire housing delivery process, not merely the time or labor required to assemble a unit in a factory.

Notably, BOXABL announced that on October 27th, it signed a contract to sell 20 Casitas to Kaw Gaming, Inc., a Native American tribe in Oklahoma, and just yesterday issued a press release saying that shipment of those orders began last week, with more shipping this week. If that short timeline from order to shipment indicates that it is shipping finished inventory, that would certainly be a positive sign for deliveries, cash flow, and inventory management.

Sources indicate that BOXABL’s July Nasdaq listing provided access to public equity markets but not the large infusion of unrestricted operating cash the tech giant likely hoped for. After shareholder redemptions, the business combination generated approximately $47.2 million in gross trust proceeds. About $31.1 million was allocated to obligations under an equity prepaid forward transaction, and additional closing costs reduced the net increase in unrestricted cash to approximately $6.5 million.

Sources indicate that the firm established an at-the-market stock (ATM) offering program on September 25th, authorizing up to $100 million in equity sales. As of November 6, the company had generated about $646,000 in gross proceeds from the stock issuance. Notably, the program was initiated in late September, when the stock traded just under $4 per share.

The company issued very little equity in the six weeks after initiating the program (when the stock was at a higher price, relative to the November 24th closing price of $0.95), but some of this likely reflects restrictions on issuance during the quiet period before reporting results for the quarter.

In a recent development, management believes that existing cash, product sales, forward-transaction proceeds, and future equity sales can fund operations for the next 12 months. The manufacturer also reported approximately $2.7 million in additional forward-transaction receipts from October 1 to November 6. Given recent trends, it appears unlikely that the company will become cash flow positive from operations in the near term. In addition, with the stock now trading below $1 per share, issuing equity at this level would not generate significant capital and would send a worrisome signal about the company’s liquidity.

Those resources provide some financial flexibility, but the gap between authorization to raise capital and actually securing it remains significant. BOXABL can continue cutting costs, seek additional financing or strategic partners, focus on markets with more favorable delivery conditions, and prioritize converting finished inventory into revenue.

It has been revealed that each alternative involves trade-offs. Cutting expenses preserves cash but can constrain efforts to accelerate deliveries. Slowing production reduces near-term spending but weakens overhead absorption. Raising equity extends the operating runway but may dilute existing shareholders. Narrowing the company’s product or geographic focus could improve execution while postponing the scale central to its original economic proposition.

These are not necessarily signs of an inevitable endpoint. They are choices facing a capital-dependent manufacturer whose commercial progress has not yet matched the resources needed to sustain operations. The longer that gap persists, the more difficult it becomes to preserve every element of the company’s original ambitions.

Sources indicate that experienced homebuilding leaders approach industrialized construction ventures with both interest and skepticism, for good reason. They recognize the efficiency potential of factory production. They also know that housing profitability depends on capital allocation, customer demand, regulatory compliance, construction execution, and cash conversion.

Those disciplines become more demanding when borrowing costs remain elevated, input costs are under pressure, and homebuyers demand concessions to overcome affordability constraints.

Recent findings suggest that BOXABL’s financial challenges do not invalidate industrialized construction. Different approaches to modular production, panelization, and off-site manufacturing entail distinct capital requirements and operating models.

But its latest disclosures illustrate how difficult it can be to translate manufacturing innovation into a financially sustainable housing enterprise. The next several quarters will show whether BOXABL can accelerate deliveries, reduce inventory exposure, improve manufacturing margins, and secure sufficient liquidity without further constraining its flexibility.

The company has made some progress in slowing its cash outflow, and those improvements deserve recognition. It also continues to operate at a substantial loss, consuming considerably more cash than its products generate and depending on financial and operational improvements that remain uncertain.

BOXABL’s challenge is no longer primarily to persuade investors and customers that industrialized housing could transform residential construction. It is to demonstrate, through completed deliveries, disciplined working-capital management, and eventually positive cash flow, that its approach can sustain a business.

The company’s recent hiring may indicate that it’s doing all it can to deliver on this. Since September 15th, the company has hired Larry King as Chief Financial Officer, Heather Clayton as Chief Accounting Officer, Josef Elimlich to oversee sales strategy and the structure and performance of the sales organization, and Antonio Gonzalez as director of home delivery. While the company likely should have had the right people in these roles some time ago, the hires may indicate that it recognizes its challenges and is working to resolve them.

Sources indicate that in homebuilding, being built for difficult conditions means more than having a promising product or innovative manufacturing process. It means having an operating model that can produce, deliver, and earn its way forward when capital is expensive, buyers are cautious, and the market offers little forgiveness for execution problems.

Sources indicate that that’s a standard BOXABL, founded in 2017 and boasting having raised more than $230 million from more than 50,000 investors, now must meet. Otherwise, it will join scores of prior valiant, promising, deeply-funded ventures that got caught in the echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet.

Key Financial & Operational Highlights.

It has been revealed that HONG KONG, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- RoboSense Technology Co., Ltd ("RoboSense" or the "Organization") (HKEX: 02498), a pioneering robotics technology platform company for Physical AI, today announced its unaudited financial results for the nine months ended September 30, 2026.

Space Camera Enters Supply Chains of Leading Global AI Companies.

It has been revealed that roboSense's Space Camera has been showcased at major robotics conferences, including ICRA, IROS and CoRL, gaining widespread recognition across academia and industry. The Company has entered the supply chains of several leading global AI companies and established collaborations with leading AI model developers in North America and several leading humanoid robotics companies worldwide. Its products have been granted testing validation certificates by several leading customers, paving the way for future deployment at scale.

Space Camera is becoming a gateway for robots to acquire real-world spatial data, serving both data collection and humanoid robot applications. For data collection, RoboSense is working with AI model companies and data collection partners to validate egocentric data capture and motion capture. For humanoid robots, Space Camera serves as their eyes, supporting mobility and dexterous manipulation. Consistent perception across both applications helps bridge the gap between model training and real-world deployment.

Robotics LiDAR Growth and Customer Expansion.

Sales volume of LiDAR products for robotics and others reached approximately 427,800 units in the first nine months of 2026, up about 423.0% year over year. RoboSense continues to expand its digital LiDAR applications across commercial cleaning, autonomous delivery, embodied robotics and 3D spatial data collection.

In a recent development, as robots move from demonstrations to real-world applications, RoboSense is focused on improving product reliability and integration efficiency, while leveraging its existing robotics customer base to support the commercialization of new products. The integration of E2 and EM4 with NVIDIA Holoscan Sensor Bridge further expands its robotics development ecosystem.

ADAS LiDAR Sales and Vehicle Adoption.

LiDAR sales volume for ADAS applications reached approximately 866,900 units in the first nine months, up about 133.9% year over year. As of September 30, RoboSense had secured design wins for 197 vehicle models with 36 automotive OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers, with 91 models having achieved SOP. The company aims to expand digital LiDAR adoption into vehicles in mainstream price segments and increase LiDAR content value per vehicle through a combination of main LiDAR and blind-spot LiDAR.

This strategy is supported by advancements in RoboSense's in-house semiconductor chips and manufacturing capabilities. The first vehicle model equipped with LiDAR powered by RoboSense's Phoenix SPAD-SoC chip entered mass production and began deliveries in November 2026. In the same month, RoboSense commissioned the world's first fully automated digital LiDAR production line in Shenzhen. The line has an overall automation rate of 99% and an annual production capacity of 500,000 units, and requires only six operators at the final assembly stage.

RoboSense (HKEX: 02498) is a pioneering robotics technology platform company for Physical AI. Founded in 2014 and headquartered in Shenzhen, China, the company has offices in Shanghai, Suzhou, Hong Kong, Munich, Detroit, Silicon Valley, and other locations.

Built on its in-house optoelectronic chips, perception algorithms, and automotive-grade mass production capabilities, RoboSense provides core robotics components, including digital LiDAR and RGB-D Space Cameras.

It has been revealed that its digital LiDAR products have been deployed across more than ten application areas, including intelligent driving, autonomous delivery, robotic lawn mowing, and embodied intelligence. The tech giant ranks No. 1 globally in robotics LiDAR market share.

Looking ahead, through the scaled deployment of Space Camera, digital LiDAR and other products, RoboSense will expand the use of its Space Cameras and digital LiDAR to collect data for robot learning and provide onboard sensing, building the perception foundation for Physical AI.

#122071. How real estate agents handle proof of funds and disclosures

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1172 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

How real estate agents handle proof of funds and disclosures

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a recent coaching call this week, an agent asked a question that looks tactical and is actually about professional discipline.
  • Let me give the coaching first, because the sequence is where most agents go wrong.
  • Proof of funds gets requested too early and in the wrong tone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a recent coaching call this week, an agent asked a question that looks tactical and is actually about professional discipline. She works mostly in commercial, she has a physician buying a home and several of her clients have investors behind them, which makes gathering proof of funds a real ordeal. When do I ask for it? Does it need to be current? And how do I protect something that private? Those questions sit squarely on the line between being a salesperson and being a fiduciary, and that line is where our industry keeps getting tested.

Let me give the coaching first, because the sequence is where most agents go wrong.

Proof of funds gets requested too early and in the wrong tone. Imagine a buyer who just called on an ad. If the first thing you do is hand them a list of documents, you have converted a warm first contact into homework, and you have done it before you have given them a single reason to trust you. I do not open any client relationship by burdening the person with tasks. The order has to serve the relationship, not the file.

Here is the sequence I teach. Get them into the office first. On that opening call you can ask one soft question, do you happen to have a proof of funds ready, and if the answer is no, you keep it light. We will need it at some point, bring it when we meet if you can, but do not worry about it now. You have raised the flag without turning it into a barrier.

When they arrive, run a genuine buyer appointment and get the buyer to hire you, the same way you would work to get hired by a seller. Only then do you assign the homework, and now the identical list that would have felt like a wall on the phone lands as a initiative. Here is what we need from you, and in the meantime let’s define exactly what you are looking for, let me show you what is available, and we can even see a couple so you get a feel for the market. The serious looking begins once I have the documents. The buyer never feels interrogated. They feel represented.

Powerfact: You earn the right to ask for documents by first earning the relationship.

Now to the part that matters for leaders, because it is about how we protect our businesses and our clients at the same time.

She asked whether to send buyers to their own bank or recommend someone she knows. I prefer to recommend my own lender, and I say that carefully, because we are operating in a litigation environment, and the professional move is to assume you could be sued and to run your business so that you are covered. Practically, that means disclosing any financial relationship in writing, every time. On our coaching platform I built a document I call the Transparency Conversation, a simple editable form that states who you are connected to, how you get paid, and whether anyone shares in a fee. If the lender is tied to your organization and a financial arrangement exists, that gets disclosed plainly. If you are recommending someone purely because you know and trust the loan officer, you say exactly that and nothing more.

Industry observers note that here is how I used to present the recommendation itself, and the logic has aged well. You can use any lender you want, that is your call. The reason I like my person is this. I could refer a lot of lenders, and I choose this one, because if he ever lets you down, he does not just lose your loan, he loses every piece of business I will ever send him. So he will do whatever it takes, within the rules, to get you to the closing table. That framing respects the buyer’s freedom and explains why your recommendation carries weight. It is service, stated out loud.

According to recent reports, her question was about confidentiality. She had a buyer with roughly $2 million in proof of funds, and people are private about money at that level. Does it become confidential? Do we keep the figure quiet even though we hold the documentation?

This is where the fiduciary line gets drawn. The moment a buyer hires you, they stop being a customer and become a client, and that shift carries a duty. Anything they share with you stays with you unless they authorize otherwise. So think like an attorney. When the information is this sensitive, you protect it with a document. Have the client sign an authorization that permits you to share their financial information only with the parties who truly need it to assemble the transaction. You can adapt the Transparency Conversation form for exactly this. Now you can do your job, the client’s privacy is respected, and you have a record that protects both of you.

Another agent remarked she never provides proof of funds until after an offer is accepted. That is a sound default in many cases, but it depends on the seller. On luxury homes, estates, and commercial property, the listing side will often require proof of funds before they open the door, and that is legitimate. Sellers of a multimillion dollar property do not want a stream of non-buyers touring for decorating ideas or dream-board photos. When you represent that buyer, prepare them for the requirement so a reasonable request does not feel like an insult.

Industry observers note that for brokers and team leaders, here is the translation. Our industry has spent two years being told that our compensation and our value must be disclosed, documented, and justified. Good. The agents who will thrive under that scrutiny are the ones who already behave like fiduciaries by habit, not the ones who treat disclosure as a form to dodge. Teach your people the sequence, relationship first, documents second. Standardize the written disclosures so no agent is improvising a legal boundary on the fly. And model the confidentiality, because a buyer who sees you guard their two million dollar statement like it is your own will refer you for the rest of their life.

Recent findings suggest that the whole thing fits on one page. Do not lead with the paperwork. Get them in, get them to hire you, assign the homework as part of the service. Recommend your lender, and disclose everything in writing. Treat their financial information as a fiduciary, with a signed authorization. And read the other side of the transaction, so you know when a request for proof is simply professionalism doing its job.

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.
  • The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Recent findings suggest that sister will provide. True, French Gates remarked, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

In a recent development, she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Latest America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Industry observers note that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers mentioned they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

Industry observers note that “Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The Fresh York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

  • Online consumer-direct lender Real Genius, which was originally a division of FirstBank, will operate as a division of Luminate Bank and remain as a consumer-facing brand.
  • Nathan Raich, executive vice president of mortgage lending at Luminate Bank, said the move is aimed at giving borrowers more flexibility in how they work with the institution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minneapolis-based Luminate Bank has agreed to acquire select assets and the mortgage origination operations of Real Genius, expanding the bank’s reach into the digital mortgage channel, the companies revealed Wednesday.

Online consumer-direct lender Real Genius, which was originally a division of FirstBank, will operate as a division of Luminate Bank and remain as a consumer-facing brand. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Nathan Raich, executive vice president of mortgage lending at Luminate Bank, said the move is aimed at giving borrowers more flexibility in how they work with the institution.

It has been revealed that “Some homebuyers want a mortgage professional beside them at every step, while others prefer a more self-directed, digital experience,” Raich said in a statement. “Mortgage lending isn’t becoming exclusively digital or exclusively relationship-driven. The opportunity is to be great at both and give customers the freedom to choose.”.

Luminate Bank was formed after a team of mortgage executives acquired the bank in 2020, with a strategy of building a “concierge” financial experience that blends traditional mortgage lending with depository services, co-founder and president of mortgage lending Eric Lovins said in a recent interview with HousingWire’s Reverse Mortgage Daily.On the Real Genius deal, Lovins said that Luminate has been working on integration planning and evaluating the organizational structure.

“Our focus is on creating a strong platform for sustainable, profitable growth while ensuring we have the right people, resources and infrastructure to support the business,” he mentioned.

Sources indicate that according to Lovins, Real Genius’s leadership team previously helped build and operate FirstBank’s ConsumerDirect mortgage platform, which delivered more than 50,000 loans over nine years and contributed to a mortgage business that generated approximately $6 billion in annual production. In 2012, the division of FirstBank became Real Genius under the leadership of CEO Jamie Thornton.

“We see tremendous value in that experience and the opportunity to build on it,” Lovins mentioned.

It has been revealed that he added that the deal leverages Luminate’s broader mortgage and banking platform and represents another key step in expanding its national mortgage presence. The manufacturer’s strategy continues to focus on both organic growth and strategic acquisitions.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, Luminate acquired assets of Illinois-based First State Mortgage Services, extending its footprint across the Midwest and central U.S. Many members of First State Mortgage’s team, led by CEO and president Rene Shaffer, joined Luminate.

Luminate has originated about $3.8 billion year to date, according to mortgage technology platform InGenius. The manufacturer had 433 sponsored loan officers as of Wednesday, per the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System.

According to recent reports, in December 2022, Luminate Home Loans — a subsidiary of the bank that has operated since 1998 — brought the more than 200-member NEO Home Loans team, previously part of Celebrity Home Loans, onto its platform. This boosted Luminate’s distributed retail presence at a time when many independent mortgage banks were contracting.

According to recent reports, in October 2024, however, Luminate revealed that it would shut down the NEO Home Loans division. The company noted the decision was driven by a desire to “focus on integrating mortgage lending into its core banking services to better serve clients and build long-term financial relationships.” The NEO group is now partnered with AI-focused mortgage lender Better.com.

Bitcoin (BTC), the world’s largest cryptocurrency, has recorded a multi-month high in daily trading volume as the cryptocurrency market remains in the grip of extreme volatility.

The massive spike in trading volume comes in the wake of one of the biggest sell-offs in BTC this year.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 21, the world’s largest cryptocurrency dropped as low as around $55,100, a level last seen in September 2024. Following the sharp plunge, Bitcoin managed to make a stunning comeback as the flagship cryptocurrency recovered to trade back above $60,000 and briefly pushed toward the $61,000 mark.

The comeback, however, was short-lived as BTC lost ground again and tanked below the crucial $60,000 mark.

BTC is at the moment trading at around $58,879, rising 5.4% in the last 24 hours, as per the latest data from CoinGecko.

Furthermore, the world’s largest cryptocurrency has a 24-hour trading volume of around $43.8 billion and has regained a market cap of $1.18 trillion.

As per data from analytics firm CoinGlass, Bitcoin (BTC) futures trading volume stands at around $76.17 billion. On the other hand, the cryptocurrency's spot trading volume stands at $7.91 billion over the past 24 hours.

Despite the latest recovery, it is still trading 9.74% lower over the past seven days and more than 27% lower over the past month.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency is also down around 53.3% from its all-time high of $126,198.

Another massive wave of liquidations has swept through the cryptocurrency market following the latest recovery.

As per the latest data from CoinGlass, 85,533 traders have been liquidated in the last 24 hours, with total liquidations amounting to $562.12 million.

It is worth noting that around $406.13 million in liquidations were on the short side, while only $156 million were on the long side.

With regard to BTC, it alone accounts for around $346.18 million in liquidations, and a staggering 76.7% of those liquidations were on the bearish side.

At the moment, Bitcoin is unable to reclaim the $60,000 level with conviction.

#122064. Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1496 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Recent findings suggest that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Upcoming York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

In a recent development, his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be remarked for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan remarked. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Industry observers note that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

According to recent reports, “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he remarked. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Industry observers note that sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it revealed cold.

According to recent reports, “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

According to recent reports, for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and latest construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Sources indicate that andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney mentioned.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She indicates music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Industry observers note that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

According to recent reports, marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein remarked.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

Sources indicate that “Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he noted. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Sources indicate that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she stated.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith noted on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Industry observers note that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

In a recent development, howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it rolled out publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

Recent findings suggest that the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

Better Home & Finance Holding Co. signed an agreement with an unnamed mortgage servicer to offer home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans to existing borrowers, expanding its lead-generation channels as the manufacturer continues its turnaround efforts.

The agreement, revealed Tuesday in the company’s Week 7 Better 2.0 scorecard, is expected to provide a lower-cost customer acquisition channel.

Since its Week 6 scorecard on Nov. 17, Better has identified additional efficiencies across its corporate organization that are expected to generate a total of $38.97 million in annualized savings. The company also reported $770,000 in additional annualized savings from mortgage operations.

Better said it plans to pursue another $1.5 million in vendor-related reductions by Dec. 1. The tech giant is working toward a broader cost savings target of $64.2 million.

“HELOC volume with our partners continues to grow each week, four more brokerages are lined up to join our wholesale platform, and two fresh partnerships are set to launch. At the same time, we’re moving toward a signed agreement to sell Birmingham Bank, which will let us focus fully on our U.S. business,” said Vishal Garg, Better’s founder and head of product, platform and innovation.

The tech giant has received five term sheets for about $50 million in debt financing tied to the proposed sale of the bank and is continuing discussions with prospective financing partners.

The company mentioned its AI-powered HELOC partnership with a large existing customer is live, with volume increasing weekly. Better is also preparing a multichannel campaign to expand the product through its wholesale platform and onboard additional brokerages.

According to recent reports, four more mortgage brokerages are in the pipeline to join the platform. Two previously announced partnerships — with a rental credit management platform and a home inspection manufacturer — are expected to launch early next week.

Better is also advancing discussions with three other major partners and a previously revived large-scale partnership, its release stated.

Bitcoin (BTC) bull and SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci has argued that the world's biggest cryptocurrency could find a critical bottom as soon as this week.

Scaramucci's comments follow the leading cryptocurrency's struggle to recover from a catastrophic crypto market crash that took BTC to its lowest price level in over two years.

It has been revealed that in the latest episode of All Things Markets on Nov. 20, the SkyBridge Capital founder joined Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz to discuss a potential bottom for Bitcoin.

It has been revealed that scaramucci shared his view that Bitcoin could see its bottom on Nov. 25, citing the cryptocurrency's four-year halving cycle as the driving force behind his comments.

"Before we came on, I asked ChatGPT when's the expected halving for Bitcoin," Scaramucci explained.

Sources indicate that "And then when are we 500 days out from that halving? And the estimate was November 25th," he added.

This prediction stems from the idea that Bitcoin's price trends could follow a predictable four-year cycle that coincides with the cryptocurrency's halving events, when the newly introduced BTC supply is cut in half.

This theory suggests that Bitcoin could find its major bottom around the 500-day mark before its next halving, expected in 2028.

However, these theories are by no means a certainty when it comes to predicting future price action, especially with the current level of institutional participation and macroeconomic forces impacting the crypto market to an unprecedented extent.

During the conversation, Novogratz also took note of Bitcoin's history of forming double bottoms during its four-year cycles.

"And every four years, Bitcoin double bottomed," Novogratz remarked.

At the time, the Galaxy Digital CEO's comments suggested a potentially positive scenario, as Bitcoin had been able to hold its psychological $60,000 price level.

"If it doesn't break 60, that could be a good sign," he noted.

Unfortunately for Bitcoin, the cryptocurrency subsequently crashed below this critical price point. This has left some wondering whether the cryptocurrency has already found its ultimate bottom.

During the same conversation, Novogratz suggested that Bitcoin's short-term outlook could largely depend on the current situation in the stock market.

Specifically, the billionaire stated that a rebound in tech stocks could lead to a strong rally in Bitcoin's price.

It has been revealed that "If we put in a bottom in the next couple days in the S&P here, down 3% from here, down 5% from here. And we have a rally back up. Man, Bitcoin is going to rally hard with it," Novogratz predicted.

However, he also warned that Bitcoin could see a lot of market-driven movements going forward, as opposed to crypto-specific movements.

"I think we're going to be stuck tethered to general sentiment and risk," he noted.

Novogratz also believes that Bitcoin could trade in a range between $60,000 and $75,000 before a breakout or breakdown becomes apparent.

Bitcoin plunged to around $55,100 on Nov. 21, its lowest price level since September 2024, following another severe wave of sell-offs in the crypto market.

It then bounced back strongly to climb above $60,000 again, albeit briefly, before falling back to around $59,000 on Nov. 22.
