New York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“It’s my job to put Newly introduced York families first,” said Hochul, who explained as a mother and grandmother the matter is “deeply personal.” Hochul added that some of the wayward toys on the market at the moment have engaged children in “inappropriate conversations,” while some may also manipulate a child’s feelings or put their privacy at risk.

Hochul has been vocal about the dangers of AI for some time, recently imposing the first statewide moratorium on new data centers and last month signing a bill titled “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors,” which will prohibit firms from developing chatbots that feature elements that could be harmful to minors.

  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Recent findings suggest that zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Recent findings suggest that nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles stated.

Industry observers note that boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

In a recent development, retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “notable step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson stated in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Recent findings suggest that next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

It has been revealed that the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The tech giant is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

It has been revealed that since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The organization has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

Upcoming solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure.

It has been revealed that LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing upcoming demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The organization also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies.

From the source grid to the cabinet: an integrated AIDC power architecture.

In a recent development, during the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management.

Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the tech giant describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE.

Recent findings suggest that the solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle.

It has been revealed that the system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life.

Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE notes the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years.

Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications.

The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications.

Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds.According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less.

Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC.

Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly introduced AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the organization's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration.

According to recent reports, the integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when problems arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock.

According to recent reports, EVE claims it ranked No. 2 globally in energy-storage cell shipments in the first half of 2026. The organization reports cumulative global shipments of 230 GWh and inclusion in S&P Global's Tier 1 list of energy storage system integrators. Building on its strategy of "global manufacturing, global cooperation and global service," EVE says it will continue developing grid-forming capabilities and energy storage products for the full range of AIDC applications. The company aims to become a trusted global energy partner for AI computing infrastructure, supporting reliable and lower-carbon power for the AI era.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn’t look like a typical candidate for state housing help.
  • The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority launched a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers.
  • It has been revealed that colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn’t look like a typical candidate for state housing help. In Colorado, if that borrower is a firefighter, emergency medical technician or police officer, the person now qualifies.

The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority launched a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers. CHFA Colorado Champions uses a newly introduced state law that raises income limits for eligible borrowers.

It has been revealed that colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers. The goal is to give them more chances to live near where they serve. Maryland, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Texas, Florida and South Carolina also offer similar programs.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont unveiled a fresh homeownership assistance program for first responders. It offers up to $25,000 in forgivable down payment and closing cost assistance. The program stems from a law Lamont signed this year.

“By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them,” Lamont remarked in a statement.

CHFA Colorado Champions arrives as the housing market weakens, following several years of zoning and regulatory reform.

According to recent reports, colorado’s single-family housing market has been steadily cooling since spring, according to HousingWire Intelligence data through Nov. 20. Inventory peaked in September and has barely eased, while median list prices have fallen since July. Homes are also taking longer to sell, with days on market rising since late July and price reductions staying elevated.

In a recent development, the latest weekly figures show no reversal, with single-family homes taking a median 91 days to sell, up from 84. The median single-family list price is $599,000, and about 48% of single-family listings carry price cuts, the data show.

Lawmakers have spent years trying to improve affordability, mostly by loosening local land-use rules. In 2024, Gov. Jared Polis signed laws requiring more density near transit and clearing the way for accessory dwelling units. The package also removed some parking minimums for urban multifamily housing and lifted limits on unrelated people living together.

A law Polis signed this year requires towns with more than 2,000 people to allow housing on certain small parcels. Eligible land belongs to school districts, colleges, transit districts, housing authorities and qualifying nonprofits. The law takes effect Dec. 31, 2027, while lot-size bills failed in the Legislature this year.

Senate Bill 26-053, a bipartisan law, raised CHFA’s mortgage income limits to 110% of standard guidelines. That allows eligible borrowers earning up to $196,810 a year to qualify.

According to recent reports, the program offers a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage. The program covers down payment and closing costs up to the lesser of $25,000 or 4% of the first mortgage. Borrowers apply through a CHFA participating lender.

It has been revealed that the aid is a second mortgage. Repayment is deferred until the term ends, the first mortgage is paid off, or the borrower sells, refinances or moves.

CHFA Executive Director Thomas Bryan remarked in a statement that first responders keep communities safe. Many can’t afford local homes, he added.

Industry observers note that “They should be able to live where they serve,” Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, one of the law’s sponsors, said in a statement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • Sources indicate that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

Sources indicate that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The firm started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond manufacturer agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

In a recent development, the five-year-old firm was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he noted.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has noted it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Recent findings suggest that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents remarked.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

According to recent reports, pierpoint stated he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

Sources indicate that white also allegedly stated that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton mentioned it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or strategy.”.

Recent findings suggest that pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also mentioned the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” mentioned David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

Climate Action Integrated into Business Decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being declared, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what’s happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs.

It has been revealed that as we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since.

Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.

Industry observers note that purchase application data, on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization.

Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down massive, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December.

Sources indicate that latest home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it’s still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates.

In a recent development, one positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long.

As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%.

According to recent reports, if we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday!

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid swiftly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

According to recent reports, underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

According to recent reports, “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he remarked. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

In a recent development, after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

Industry observers note that “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

According to recent reports, redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In a recent development, in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

It has been revealed that he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

It has been revealed that redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he noted, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

According to recent reports, in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd remarked, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

Industry observers note that A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The manufacturer landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Sources indicate that team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Sources indicate that endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd mentioned there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The tech giant now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

In a recent development, “This was always the end goal,” Redd noted. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Ethereum developers want to change the gas accounting for validator deposits. The blueprint is to measure the request bytes that these deposit events create.

The gas calculation already accounts for executing a deposit. However, after the deposit is finished, a 192-byte request is passed along with the block. Those 192 bytes are excluded from the minimum gas charge, so the same gas limit might allow more data than the initial calculation accounts for.

Under Gloas, there is no fixed cap on the number of deposit requests per block. The execution layer has not capped this either. Gas is the only limiting factor.

It has been revealed that neither EIP-8131 nor EIP-8279 accounts for those request bytes. This means that deposits could become another way to bypass the gas floor once EIP-8279 closes the loophole involving cold storage reads.

According to recent reports, A relay contract can call the deposit contract repeatedly, costing around 26,000 gas per deposit. In the author's example, that execution cost is below the point where the gas floor for zero-byte calldata would start to increase the total charge.

This results in a payload of about 1.44 times the block gas limit divided by 64, compared with about 1.15 times the same baseline.

The main issue is the data size, so the proposal directly addresses the data.

Industry observers note that A log from the deposit contract with the deposit event topic counts as 192 bytes before the log entry is added. This is the same condition EIP-6110 uses to turn logs into requests.

The cost of this would be another check that client developers would have to implement and test.

It has been revealed that consumers are not expected to pay more for regular deposits. The cost of executing a regular deposit is already above the proposed minimum, so the extra 12,288 gas only raises the minimum charge.

The proposal has yet to be scheduled for a network upgrade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

In a recent development, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of upcoming homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

Industry observers note that october’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement.

Fresh home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the fresh home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

Sources indicate that for example, mortgage applications for latest-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

In a recent development, “Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s newly introduced home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”.

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

Sources indicate that last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in new orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Industry observers note that sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,.

Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon stated during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

In a recent development, “Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he noted during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

“Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi noted, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BEIJING, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The large-scale deployment of LLMs inevitably involves challenges at two levels: at the top is end-to-end inference efficiency, and at the bottom are operators. As model parameter counts continue to grow and inference costs become a bottleneck to deployment, the way an inference framework organizes computation, schedules memory, and manages communication determines how much throughput and latency the same hardware can deliver. Ultimately, all these system-level optimizations must be implemented through operators. High-performance operators are the foundational layer for reducing inference latency, increasing throughput, and unlocking the potential of heterogeneous computing hardware.

In a recent development, for AI chips with different architectures, developing high-performance, deployable operators that work across chipsâand then organizing those operators into an end-to-end, production-ready inference systemâhas long ceased to be an internal concern for any single chip manufacturer. It is now an engineering hurdle shared by AI systems developers.

The FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition (Season 2) was designed to address precisely this gap. Season 2 featured two independent tracks that complemented each other, spanning low-level operators and system-level inference. Track 1 focused on optimizing the performance of SGLang framework operators across multiple AI chips. More than 200 operators from real inference workloads were released in batches, testing participants' ability to perform deep operator-level optimization across chips. Track 2 shifted its focus to the end-to-end inference throughput of ModelBest models. Using the FlagOS inference framework and the FlagGems operator library, participants were required to perform full-stack optimization of the MiniCPM5-2B model on Iluvatar CoreX and MetaX chips, pushing the upper limit of total tokens/s.

It has been revealed that one track went deep into operators, while the other tackled the full system stack. Together, they provided a comprehensive test of FlagOS's cross-chip capabilities. Over the four-month competition from July to November 2026, Season 2 attracted 2,025 participants worldwide, including 146 participants from outside China. A total of 72,125 submissions were received, of which 354 were valid.

According to recent reports, the competition brought forward many development teams and individual developers whose work deserves to be documented. Those who reached the podium did not fit a single profile: they included a small industry team working on inference acceleration for video-generation models, an individual developer working alone with AI Agents, a student who persevered despite limited hardware access, and a returning veteran who had competed in both seasons and refined his methods in his spare time. They started with different resources and took different paths. The following accounts document how several of them entered the competition, the difficulties they faced, the solutions they developed, and what they gained from the experience.

According to recent reports, I. An Experienced Industry Team: Using Controlled Measurements to Bring "Intuition" Back Down to Earth.

The c2flow R&D team at Yusuan Intelligence has long worked on accelerating world-model inference. In team member Zhang Pengfei's words, its core task is to make video-generation models run faster. Operator fusion and optimization are already part of the team's day-to-day work, so when his team saw information about the competition on the FlagOS WeChat account and at WAIC, they rapidly concluded that the challenges closely matched their own work. The team began preparing during the first week after registration opened.

Zhang Pengfei explained that the team's division of labor happened to cover several of the hardest parts of the competition, including setting up the Agent environment, diagnosing problems, and improving productivity with AI. Even so, the team encountered many obstacles. Zhang recalled that, during the early stages of the competition, compilation failures occurred frequently while adapting operators for Kunlunxin. Even when compilation succeeded, the computed results sometimes failed to match the reference implementation. The team later discovered that compilation did not require access to physical hardware, so it changed its process to run compilation checks locally first, eliminating environment-related complications earlier. To investigate accuracy discrepancies, the team later borrowed a Kunlunxin P800 and repeatedly validated its implementations on the actual device, significantly improving the efficiency of problem diagnosis.

Recent findings suggest that A controlled experiment on Problem 144 illustrates the team's strong technical foundation. The implementation used several sophisticated techniques, including packing two 16-bit values into one 32-bit value for data movement, which intuition suggested should have been the main source of acceleration. However, after testing each change separately on the same chip, the team found that packing delivered no measurable benefit. What actually mattered was a small cache hint for reads and writes, which improved overall performance on the task by approximately 24%. To rule out measurement noise, the team alternated four submissions during the same periodâtwo with the hint and two without itâand the results within each pair matched.

Recent findings suggest that this experiment changed the order in which the team evaluated optimization results. Previously, its first question had been, "Can it run faster?" Afterward, the more key question became, "Can this number be reproduced?" Zhang noted the team fixed its evaluation criteria in advance: candidates that produced incorrect results would not generate performance numbers. It first established the validation system and only then allowed AI to attempt optimizations at scale.

Recent findings suggest that the same approach also paid off on Task 130, the layernorm_scale_shift_gate_select01 operator challenge. The team's first submission achieved an average speedup of 4.01Ã, which appeared substantial, but it failed to meet the threshold because performance on one chip was only 0.05Ã. The team then changed strategies and wrote a dedicated implementation for each of the five chips, raising the average speedup to 11.65Ã and successfully completing a "Validated Solve." This result also points to a counterintuitive conclusion: the best solution for cross-chip optimization is often not a single universal implementation, but multiple specialized implementations for different hardware platforms under FlagOS's unified interface.

According to the team's statistics, over the course of the three-plus-month competition, c2flow achieved 114 "First Solves" among 211 challengesâthe number of operators for which it was first to produce an implementation that met the challenge requirementsâand 100 "Validated Solves"âthe number of operators that passed the judges' review and met the development requirements. All 100 validated implementations have been merged into the official FlagGems-sglang repository. Discussing future plans, Zhang said the team would extend its work from operator development to end-to-end inference optimization for both text-only and multimodal models, measuring results by end-to-end latency and throughput.

In a recent development, speaking about the FlagOS technology stack, Zhang praised its greatest advantage: the FlagOS ecosystem has accumulated a large number of high-performance general-purpose operator implementations that developers can use as references. Even when AI is used to assist operator development, the experience embodied in FlagOS remains extremely crucial. For example, when supporting a fresh operator, AI can begin with implementations of similar operators in FlagGems and then adjust them based on measurements from the target chip.

It has been revealed that II. A Developer with AI Agents: One Person, One Pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that yang Zhongwu of the EvokeAgent team represents another form of participation. Yang is a graduate student in Control Science and Engineering at Nankai University, and his competition team consisted of himself and his Agent assistants. He had previously worked on operator development during an internship at BAAI. He registered this time with the thought, "Let's see whether I can take a few challenges.".

Yang's competition journey followed a very clear progression. He began by using vibe coding to optimize individual operators. After completing several challenges, he started developing an automated optimization workflow. This pipeline shifted his role from "writing optimizations" to "reviewing operators and submitting them," freeing up a great deal of time and energy. But the pipeline itself also required continual patching. During his exploration, he encountered edge cases such as the compilation-cache mechanism on Huawei Ascend chips and had to update his rules to guard against them. "Everyone is using AI for optimizationâwhy should mine be better?" was the greatest challenge he felt he faced. His answer was to understand real production workflows well enough to outperform others in both process and detail.

It has been revealed that in addition, to address limited access to computing resources, Yang mainly rented online compute powered by locally developed hardware, which helped him make it through many submission windows. As more operator pull requests appeared in the FlagGems-sglang repository, he had more optimization experience to draw on. For example, launching with .run and hard-coding a segment of PTX assembly into the code could significantly improve performance on a certain type of chip. His workflow gradually became standardized: first, generate test shapes and scripts for correctness and performance testing based on repository examples; next, optimize for large, medium, and small shapes using profiling tools together with a knowledge base; and finally, incorporate upcoming knowledge from repository pull requests.

The impact of this experience on Yang was highly tangible. His strongest impression was that "one person using AI can already reach the level of a ten-person team.".

He also offered his own interpretation of FlagOS's open-computing philosophy: cross-chip operator support is not intended to eliminate hardware differences. Instead, FlagOS's unified AI systems software stack is designed to make full use of the performance advantages of different hardware platforms, enable technical achievements to be reused across platforms, and allow developers to move from compatibility work to innovation.

III. A Veteran of Two Seasons: The Regret of Missing by Seconds, and a Knowledge Base That Grows by Itself.

Industry observers note that like Yang Zhongwu of EvokeAgent, Zhou Chunguang, who works at Alps System Integration (Dalian) Co., Ltd., entered the competition as an individual developer. Unlike Yang, however, he had already participated in the first season of the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition. Asked why he returned, Zhou mentioned that, on the one hand, he wanted to continue the experience from the previous season and use the opportunity to try fresh technologies and tools. On the other hand, the flexible schedule allowed him to keep developing, submitting, and optimizing in spare moments outside work and daily life, making the format well suited to individual developers. In addition, the gamified leaderboard provided feedback on every attempt.

But competition for a "First Solve" was more intense than he had expected. The experience that stayed with him most strongly was finally completing the development work and submitting it, only to discover that he had missed the "First Solve" by a few seconds. It was disappointing, but it also made the competition tense and engaging. Whenever this happened, he would look back and consider where he could become more efficient in preparation for the next challenge.

Zhou's core method for this competition was a continually growing knowledge base. First, he asked AI to help him understand each problem and organize possible approaches. He then used actual submissions and result feedback to determine whether a solution was correct and whether its performance met the standard. When an attempt failed, he recorded the error, its possible causes, and effective ways to address it, allowing the next attempt to benefit from previous experience. He dynamically collected lessons from each round of challenges, then continuously revised and expanded them based on latest results. The AI's ability to handle subsequent challenges improved accordingly. Rather than pursuing a dramatic breakthrough in a single round, he made every attempt leave behind a searchable asset for the next.

This method also changed his view of learning. When entering an unfamiliar technical field, it is not always necessary to wait until every piece of knowledge has been fully mastered before beginning. Instead, one can use AI to build a basic understanding, then fill in the gaps continuously through practice, validation, and review. After the competition, he aims to continue following the use of AI tools in specialized technical tasks and to explore how individual developers can learn and solve complex problems more efficiently.

His assessment of FlagOS's open-computing philosophy and cross-chip compatibility was straightforward: different hardware platforms have their own characteristics. If developers can exchange experience and validate solutions in an open software ecosystem like FlagOS, they have an opportunity to lower the barriers to compatibility work and optimization, enabling more hardware platforms and developers to participate.

IV. A Student: When Hardware Is Scarce, Make Up for It with a "To-Be-Validated List".

Compared with the other participating teams, Du Xuanzheng faced much harsher practical constraints. A student at Beihang University, he focuses on AI systems software and high-performance computing. His motivation for entering was simple: the competition offered an opportunity to practice cross-chip optimization. He wanted to test his existing programming experience on real hardware while systematically learning Triton and performance analysis.

Access to physical hardware, however, was precisely his biggest constraint. Apart from one GPU available for hands-on testing, the only other hardware he had access to was an Ascend card, leaving him unable to benchmark performance on other chips. To address this limitation, he divided the problem into two parts: for what he could verify on the GPU at his disposal, he conducted careful experiments; for chips he could not test directly, he consulted vendor documentation and open-source examples, explored potential adaptation approaches, and developed solutions pending validation. He set himself one rule: clearly distinguish measured results, evidence from documentation, and questions still awaiting validation, and never apply results from the single GPU directly to other chips.

Even when working with the GPU available to him, Du took a measured approach. For each operator, he compared different parallelization strategies and memory access patterns, aiming to test just one hypothesis at a time. He checked correctness first, repeated performance tests, and documented both successful and unsuccessful attempts. Along the way, he discovered that making code more complex does not necessarily lead to more consistent performance gains. Some approaches may seem reasonable in theory but fail to deliver the expected results in practice. He therefore became more disciplined about preserving code versions and raw results, repeating measurements for the same approach, and determining whether performance improvements were consistent. Whenever he saw a faster result, his first questions were: Why is it faster? Can the result be reproduced? He considers this habit one of the most valuable lessons he gained from the competition.

Recent findings suggest that the competition also made Du's understanding of AI development more concrete. In the past, complex low-level code could initially make the barrier to entry seem very high. Now, he tries to break it down into semantics, implementation, testing, and performance, then works through each part one by one.

According to recent reports, his experience in the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition also gave him clearer direction for his future development. He plans to focus his studies on AI systems software and high-performance computing, strengthen his knowledge of computer architecture, parallel computing, and compiler optimization, continue developing operators, and seek opportunities to work with a wider range of real hardware.

He also remarked that the most compelling aspect of FlagOS is the ability to study different chips through open operator interfaces and the Triton development model. Existing computational semantics and algorithmic approaches can be reused, while public code allows developers to compare and understand the implementation of each backend. Compared with development around a single device, this approach encourages developers to focus on how common logic connects with backend differences and provides more concrete references when they consult documentation and analyze compatibility solutions.

This year, development teams with different backgrounds participated in the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition (Season 2) in different ways.

Industry observers note that zhang Pengfei's c2flow team at Yusuan Intelligence brought the engineering discipline of an industry team, using controlled measurements to anchor every "speedup" in reproducible evidence. After the competition, it will extend these capabilities to end-to-end inference optimization. Yang Zhongwu of EvokeAgent amplified his individual productivity with an automated optimization pipeline, searching for his own place between the efficiency of "one person working like a team" and the palpable reality of employment pressure. Working with limited hardware, Du Xuanzheng used a "to-be-validated list" and experimental records to fill gaps in cross-chip assessment while clearly setting his career direction toward AI systems software. As a veteran of two seasons, Zhou Chunguang patiently turned his spare time into a knowledge base that continues to grow.

Recent findings suggest that what they share is not simply that "they all won awards," but that they genuinely developed cross-chip operator optimization capabilities through this competition. This did not depend on any single talent. It emerged from repeatedly raising questions, testing judgments, and revising solutions under the combined constraints of correctness requirements, chip differences, and leaderboard pressure.

Although the FlagOS Open Computing Global Competition (Season 2) has concluded, the next batch of challenges, the next group of developers, and the next round of cross-chip challenges are already on the way. The FlagOS community's positioning of the competitionâ"advancing R&D through competition, energizing the ecosystem through competition, and cultivating talent and setting benchmarks through competition"âhas found concrete expression in the stories of these developers.

To support the large-scale deployment of different AI chips, BAAI joined with research institutions, chip companies, system vendors, and organizations working in algorithms and softwareâboth in China and abroadâto initiate and establish the FlagOS community. It now has more than 100 member organizations.

In a recent development, flagOS is an open-source, cross-chip systems software stack designed for AI chips. It enables AI models to be developed once and seamlessly ported to a wide range of hardware platforms, significantly reducing migration and compatibility costs. Its core open-source projects include a large-scale operator library, a cross-chip AI compiler, a parallel training and inference framework, and a cross-chip communication library. It is committed to building an open technology ecosystem spanning the model, system, and chip layers, unlocking hardware computing potential through "develop once, migrate across chips," and breaking down ecosystem silos among the software stacks of different chips.

Tech Report: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a major decision to make in the next few weeks: take the firm’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Major Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a major decision to make in the next few weeks: take the firm’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

It has been revealed that microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Industry observers note that microsoft indicates the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in newly introduced hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the firm decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a tech giant right now?

According to recent reports, harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

In a recent development, but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one tech giant.

Industry observers note that hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more key than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

Industry observers note that the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI tech giant today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Industry observers note that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual tech giant. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software tech giant.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a organization.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the significant platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue promptly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

It has been revealed that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

It has been revealed that 1) Think VERY substantial, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a manufacturer that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

Sources indicate that there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Recent findings suggest that other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Recent findings suggest that whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Significant Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?
  • According to recent reports, identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:52 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

According to recent reports, identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

Artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

AgentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

It has been revealed that language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

Sources indicate that permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

It has been revealed that agentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more vital point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

Industry observers note that the companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. Start the inventory and the permission cleanup now. The tools to enforce the rest are arriving swiftly, and they will work far better for the teams that did the groundwork.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
