📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The White House has unveiled a litany of fresh tariffs targeting imports from 14 economies, including key trading partners such as China and the EU. With consumers already stretched by an affordability crisis, the new duties come on the same day that the Bureau of Economic Analysis confirmed inflation hit 3.8%, according to the annual rate of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, and nearly double the Federal Open Market Committee’s 2% goal.

Industry observers note that the announcement has two vital implications. First, though the latest duties would be imposed on foreign economies, previous tariff studies indicate that 90% of the increased prices are ultimately borne by U.S. businesses and, more often than not, their consumers.

Sources indicate that and second, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s next move. The Fed, now led by Kevin Warsh, raised rates in September for the first time since July 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and meets again Dec. 9–10.

Sources indicate that former Fed chairman Jerome Powell stated that while tariffs represented a one-off price increase rather than broader inflationary factors, they nonetheless increased near-term inflation expectations. As UBS chief economist Paul Donovan told clients today: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates.”.

And the Fed already has a data headache on its hands: The PCE increase to 3.8% compared with a year ago is nearly double the FOMC’s 2% target.

Industry observers note that china faces a latest 20% duty, and Vietnam, up to 35%, or 20% if it reaches a trade deal, according to Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, citing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Section 301 allows the U.S. to investigate foreign practices deemed unreasonable or discriminatory, or that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Both nations are among the top 10 importers to the U.S., accounting for 7.8% and 7.4% of imports, respectively, per Census Bureau data.

It has been revealed that through September, the U.S. imported $215 billion in Chinese goods and $204.8 billion from Vietnam, which accounts for the largest U.S. trade deficit with any country, at $190.9 billion.

The European Union is also facing tariffs of 15%, while India is facing rates of up to 25%, or 17% in the event of a trade deal.

The upcoming revenue-generating tariff action comes after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs in February, forcing the administration to refund roughly $100 billion of the $166 billion it had collected.

For most of the 14 economies, existing Section 301 duties count toward the latest rate rather than being added on top. (China is the exception: Its 20% stacks on existing levies.) “In effect, it’ll look more like a top-up,” Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points.”.

That will do little to calm the nerves of consumers who have been battling above-target inflation for more than five years. The Newly introduced York Fed’s October survey of consumer expectations revealed that households expect inflation to be at 3.9% this time next year, and at 3.3% in three years’ time.

In a recent development, for the Fed, these heightened expectations can be a problem. Consumers may adjust their spending and saving, and make wage demands in response to their inflation expectations. That can create a self-reinforcing cycle, making inflation harder to bring down.

“The tariffs replace the previously confirmed Section 301 tariffs with a marginal incremental impact higher on goods prices but, moreover, set the table for further increases if negotiations break down,” Bradford Smith, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told Fortune in a note.

“The announcement serves as a reminder that the Fed’s inflation fight is exacerbated by tariffs. With inflation already an problem and the Fed awaiting the lapping of previous tariff implementations, additional tariffs will make the Fed’s job more difficult.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV mentioned that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.

He mentioned that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.

In a recent X post, Miller, who is the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, broke down why he thinks that it's easier to make an investment case for Bitcoin than for AI companies.

It has been revealed that "Bitcoin and AI owners have different expectations. The owners of AI expect companies will one day produce free cash flow. Bitcoin owners never did or will expect this," Miller stated.

And the end result is that "the valuation case is still much easier for Bitcoin than AI.".

Simply put, when investors buy stocks in AI companies, there is an expectation that at some point these companies will deliver big profits and free cash flow.

Free cash flow is the money a tech giant produces from its operations after capital expenditures. This is a significant metric for understanding the value of a company.

However, when it comes to AI companies, it can be difficult to assign a value because investors need to try to determine what kind of revenue these companies will generate, how much they will invest in infrastructure, and when these investments will start to deliver sufficient returns.

Miller has made it a point to push back against the argument that Bitcoin does not have value because it doesn't produce cash flow.

In a commentary from June 30, Miller explained that the traditional way of looking at intrinsic value, which revolves around future cash flows, doesn't really capture the potential of Bitcoin as a decentralized monetary network.

Instead, Miller said that Bitcoin's value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold.

Sources indicate that in his view, Bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold's. At least, that's what he calculated at the time.

Tech Report: Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the tech giant acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

According to recent reports, testing that more closely replicates the firm’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company indicates it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

It has been revealed that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software upgrade that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows enhancement used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

It has been revealed that so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

Sources indicate that the final report doesn’t say what the July enhancement was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report indicates.

It has been revealed that first, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Sources indicate that third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

According to recent reports, how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report claims.

Industry observers note that the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate problem.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

According to recent reports, once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft indicates it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft claims it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also intends to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Industry observers note that some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft claims its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft mentioned the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

In a recent development, the upcoming testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

It has been revealed that to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

Industry observers note that san Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor claims it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

Recent findings suggest that the next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

According to recent reports, in this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old manufacturer picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

According to recent reports, agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, unveiled a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

According to recent reports, not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of massive rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

In a recent development, typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual firm highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

In a recent development, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to matter under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

It has been revealed that the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

Recent findings suggest that for existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

Sources indicate that the Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

According to recent reports, the main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

It has been revealed that on diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board notes it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

It has been revealed that the Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

Sources indicate that the Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

According to recent reports, both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem.
  • “You take us out, and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, indicates, explaining how its chips work.
  • While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem. It marked the end of a 15-year arrangement with U.S. chipmaker Qualcomm, whose chips had been used in every iPhone since the iPhone 4, excluding some of Apple’s budget “e” series, to connect the devices to a mobile network.

“You take us out, and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, indicates, explaining how its chips work.

While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.

According to recent reports, in the year to September, Qualcomm’s total revenue fell 3% to $43.1 billion. Chip sales were down 26%, in the final three months to September.

It has been revealed that mcGuire argues the loss of Apple leaves Qualcomm less exposed to a single customer. “It’s actually very freeing when you can rebalance your customer ecosystem,” he indicates. In his view, Qualcomm’s success does not hinge on whether its chips end up in one phone maker’s handsets. “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”.

The company has meanwhile sought expansion beyond the smartphone category into the laptop, car, smart-home device, wearables, and data center markets. Revenue outside of Qualcomm’s mobile chip business is anticipated to grow by more than 60% in 2027.

Data centers remain a lucrative market for chipmakers, but it’s right now dominated by Nvidia, whose data center business accounted for 92% of revenues in its latest quarterly results.

In June, Qualcomm unveiled a new line of data center chips, and it is targeting $5 billion in data center revenue in 2027.

In a recent development, as CMO, McGuire has to persuade carmakers, computer manufacturers, and cloud companies to buy chips from a business best known for making phone modems. “We’ve diversified so much and expanded our portfolio of where we play in markets that historically we may not have been used to,” he claims. “It’s given us a really great opportunity, but it’s also obviously presented some challenges.”.

In a recent development, to manage that, he split Qualcomm into three brands, each covering a different chip depending on the buyer. Snapdragon is the firm’s consumer brand, covering the processors inside phones, laptops, and cars. Dragonwing is Qualcomm’s industrial and robotics brand, and Dragonfly, launched in June, covers Qualcomm’s data center products, including server processors and AI chips.

Recent findings suggest that qualcomm sells to device makers, rather than consumers. However, there is still an advantage to marketing to the broader public. The more people look for a Snapdragon laptop, the more chips Dell, Samsung, and others order, McGuire explains.

“Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”.

Industry observers note that this is why the brand has focused on building partnerships with sports teams, including a sponsorship deal with Manchester United, which McGuire indicates delivers exposure equal to 42 Super Bowl ads a season, and its partnership with the Mercedes Formula 1 team. McGuire says the aim is to make technology “visible and emotionally resonant.”.

This year’s holiday ad, which sees a father build a time machine using Qualcomm’s chips so his impatient son can travel forward through time to Christmas morning, takes a similar approach.

It has been revealed that “People don’t care about specs, speeds, or feeds,” McGuire notes. “They care about what technology can do for them, and they care about their passions.”.

Recent findings suggest that data center customers are a different audience, however. The people signing off on Qualcomm’s server chips are cloud companies and finance chiefs, for whom cost matters most. Here, Qualcomm competes with Nvidia on price and power use, a growing concern as data centers’ electricity demands rise. “Nobody does performance per watt better than we do,” McGuire says. Qualcomm has already signed Meta and AWS.

Running separate brands across so many markets has also stretched McGuire’s team, which he notes has not grown as fast as the manufacturer’s ambitions.

McGuire wants his team to spend 75% of its time on planned work and 25% on what he calls “dive and catch,” meaning urgent, last-minute requests. By last year, those figures had flipped, and most of the team’s time was spent firefighting. “I knew this wasn’t going to be sustainable,” he adds.

In a recent development, mcGuire believes AI will be crucial in enabling his small marketing team to keep pace with the growing list of demands. In January, McGuire tore up the department’s structure and rebuilt it around AI. “CMOs have a newly introduced role now, and that’s chief architect,” he states.

“Roles we thought were going to be crucial three to five years ago are less important today,” McGuire adds, such as production design and copywriting, which is now handled by AI agents. Meanwhile, data, strategy, and creative direction have become more important.

According to McGuire, fewer than 5% of the marketing department was affected. Most of those people moved into new roles, and a smaller number whose skills no longer matched what the team needed left. He calls it “more of a redeployment.”.

McGuire indicates the new structure is already paying off, helping to lower the organization’s reliance on agencies and reduce cycle times by two-thirds.

Industry observers note that despite all the changes, McGuire expects further upheaval in the near future. “It’s probably only going to last us 24 months. Technology is changing so fast, I’m not so naive as to think we’ve got another five years,” he adds.

His previous structure, designed in 2021, was meant to last five years but only lasted three and a half years. The department has gone from a single AI writing tool to several AI systems in three years, and McGuire sees no sign of that slowing. “Every day there’s a new tool,” he notes. “Every day they’re becoming more agentic.”.

It has been revealed that mcGuire notes that he has pushed back on demands for AI-driven cost cuts. “I don’t believe we’re at a stage right now where anyone could demand a reduction in cost because of AI,” he states. “It’s too early for that. We’re experimenting and learning.”.

Many CMOs face similar pressures. A third of marketing leaders surveyed by executive-search firm Spencer Stuart said they expected to cut headcount within two years, through AI or by eliminating redundancies.

Sources indicate that for Qualcomm, the challenge will be whether it can make the jump from phones to data centers, and whether its marketing can keep up. “If we believe we can disrupt, if we believe we have a better solution, we’re going to take a chance,” McGuire says.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. Tech Report: L.A. Lakers announce deal with Kalshi, signaling sports leagues’ growing embrace of prediction markets

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports.
  • “We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen.
  • Sources indicate that the announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports. The team announced the news on Tuesday in a brief statement that hailed the partnership, but offered few details on what it will entail.

“We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen.

Sources indicate that the announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets. The league officially embraced the platforms only a month ago, when it named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred exchanges. Kalshi has since moved quickly to turn that opening into team-level agreements, signing the Philadelphia 76ers in October before adding the Lakers this week.

Industry observers note that the NBA’s overall positioning came as something of a surprise, given that it and the National Football League had largely held back while other major sports leagues signed agreements with prediction markets. Some of these platforms let users as young as 18 wager on event contracts, with sports making up the bulk of trading.

Other major sports organizations have mostly taken a welcoming approach. The National Hockey League became the first major North American professional sports league to strike prediction market deals in October 2025, signing multiyear agreements with Kalshi and Polymarket that included rights to league data, branding, and broadcast advertising. That push expanded to more teams last week, when seven NHL teams unveiled their own marketing deals with Novig. Others, including Major League Soccer, Major League Baseball, and UFC, have also struck deals with prediction markets.

The NFL, meanwhile, has remained as the odd one out.

According to recent reports, in early October, the league filed a 24-page brief urging the Supreme Court to back state gambling regulators, who argue that sports prediction contracts should follow the same rules as traditional sports bets. At the heart of that dispute is whether the contracts are financial products governed by federal regulators or bets subject to state gambling laws. The league also raised concerns about cheating, insider trading, consumer protection, and risks to younger users.

Industry observers note that the legal fight also hangs over the Lakers’ fresh partnership. California allows tribal casinos and a state lottery, but it has kept traditional sports betting off the table, with a bookmaking ban dating back more than a century. The state kept that prohibition in place after the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports betting in 2018, and voters rejected two legalization measures in 2022.

If the Supreme Court takes up the case and sides with state regulators, Kalshi could face latest limits on offering sports contracts in California—complicating its push to reach fans in the Lakers’ home market.

Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • exchange and the app demonstrates the balance.
  • It has been revealed that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app demonstrates the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

It has been revealed that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

Industry observers note that the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

According to recent reports, for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

Recent findings suggest that the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks reveals where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

Recent findings suggest that the pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

Industry observers note that the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

According to recent reports, the SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

It has been revealed that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

Latest Update: After $26 billion in gifts, MacKenzie Scott is still worth $27 billion—and just gave Atlanta students $8 million more

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four years ago, MacKenzie Scott gave $8 million to Achieve Atlanta, a nonprofit that helps Atlanta public school students pay for and finish college.
  • Industry observers note that it is one of two gifts Scott made to Georgia education nonprofits this month, together worth $12.5 million.
  • According to recent reports, for an Atlanta Public Schools graduate pursuing a bachelor’s degree, the need-based Achieve Atlanta scholarship can be worth up to $20,000 over four years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four years ago, MacKenzie Scott gave $8 million to Achieve Atlanta, a nonprofit that helps Atlanta public school students pay for and finish college. Last week, the organization confirmed she had done it again, with a second $8 million gift that brings her total support to $16 million.

Industry observers note that it is one of two gifts Scott made to Georgia education nonprofits this month, together worth $12.5 million. The donor has given away more than $26 billion since her 2019 divorce from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, yet is still worth more than $27 billion, largely because Amazon stock keeps rising.

According to recent reports, for an Atlanta Public Schools graduate pursuing a bachelor’s degree, the need-based Achieve Atlanta scholarship can be worth up to $20,000 over four years. Students at two-year colleges and in technical programs can receive $1,500 a year for up to four semesters.

The nonprofit also helps students choose colleges, work through the application process, and find their first jobs. Since 2015, it has awarded more than $75 million in scholarships.

In a recent development, an independent evaluation by researchers affiliated with Georgia State University’s Georgia Policy Labs found that 91% of Achieve Atlanta scholars returned for a second semester of college. Among peers who also graduated from Atlanta Public Schools, had similar academic and demographic backgrounds, and enrolled in college without the program’s support, 77% did.

The gap narrows over time but holds. Six years after high school, 42% of scholars had graduated, compared with 36% of similar peers.

“The repeated investment by Scott is a testament to the success of Achieve Atlanta’s postsecondary success model,” the nonprofit said in announcing the gift.

Scott’s latest giving in Georgia also supports women returning to school later in life. The Athens-based Jeannette Rankin Foundation received $4.5 million, its largest single donation to date, according to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Karen Sterk, the foundation’s CEO, told the newspaper that its support could benefit more than a million women.

In a recent development, the two gifts fit a pattern. Scott’s higher education giving has largely bypassed elite universities in favor of HBCUs, community colleges, and tribal colleges, and her giving to historically Black colleges and universities alone has topped $1 billion, Fortune has reported.

When Scott and Bezos finalized their divorce in July 2019 after 25 years of marriage, she received roughly 4% of Amazon. The shares were worth about $37 billion then.

Since then, she has given away more than $26 billion through more than 2,700 gifts to nonprofits, according to Yield Giving, the organization she set up to make them. Forbes still estimates her net worth is more than $27 billion.

Her stake has shrunk. In the year through September 2025, Scott cut her Amazon holdings by 42%, according to a regulatory filing that did not say whether she sold, donated, or both.

But the shares she kept have kept climbing. Amazon stock gained more than 42% over the five years through July 2026, as Fortune previously reported. Those gains help explain why Scott is still worth tens of billions of dollars even as she gives away much of her fortune.

The manufacturer behind that fortune is now the largest in the U.S. by revenue. Amazon ranks No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500, ending Walmart’s 13-year run at the top.

In a recent development, scott signed the Giving Pledge in 2019, committing to give away the majority of her wealth during her lifetime or in her will. Her largest gifts include $436 million to Habitat for Humanity, $281 million to Boys & Girls Clubs of America, and $275 million to Planned Parenthood.

In a recent development, scott has also described what she wants her money to do while she still owns it. In a 2024 essay, she wrote that she asked her investment team to find funds and companies working on the same problems she supports through philanthropy. Her examples included affordable housing funds and digital health platforms for women.

When she makes a gift, she wrote, she would rather draw the money from those investments than from a stock portfolio “that increases the wealth and influence of leaders who already have it.” She wants to back ventures led by people from the communities they serve, or by founders who often struggle to raise capital, including women and people of color.

Her idea was that the same dollar could help twice: first as an investment in those ventures, and later as a donation to a nonprofit.

Sources indicate that as Scott wrote in her Giving Pledge letter, “It will take time and effort and care. But I won’t wait. And I will keep at it until the safe is empty.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy.
  • For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy.

For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources.

The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central.

According to recent reports, powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea.

Recent findings suggest that investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge.

Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 upcoming scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end.

According to recent reports, the same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end.

Sources indicate that the drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026).

According to recent reports, blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups.

We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density).

The result is a matrix highlighting:.

The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies.

The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy?

Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy.

And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook.

To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation.

While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy.

The result is a picture that indicates the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy.

To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units.

Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges.

In a recent development, early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona, a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge.

Sources indicate that notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them.

Tech Report: Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • Recent findings suggest that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Sources indicate that attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

Recent findings suggest that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley mentioned that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Sources indicate that attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals matter ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Industry observers note that could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Recent findings suggest that each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal revision at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

Industry observers note that A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Sources indicate that last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a tech giant’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

Industry observers note that it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t patch for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

In a recent development, there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

According to recent reports, former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that daily pool data reveals Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that daily pool data reveals Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to recent reports, according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

Sources indicate that zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

Industry observers note that at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

Sources indicate that the deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a upcoming transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

In a recent development, as of ZecStats' latest enhancement on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

Industry observers note that in October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Customers need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

It has been revealed that the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

Renowned financial guru and Rich Dad Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki has offered compelling insight into the reasons behind his buying spree of Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH) despite the current crypto market crash.

In a recent development, kiyosaki, who is an esteemed investor, predicts that a financial crisis could be on the horizon, and it might be even worse than the 2008 market crash. He believes that crypto assets and other hard assets are an effective hedge against the repercussions of government-induced overborrowing and money printing.

The financial guru's latest X post explains his rationale behind investing in Bitcoin, Ethereum, gold, silver, real estate, and oil instead of traditional financial assets.

"Why I am buying real (no ETFs) gold, silver, Bitcoin, and Ethereum," Kiyosaki noted in his latest post.

It has been revealed that he attributed his views to the Federal Reserve, the U.S. Treasury and the colossal debt obligations of the U.S.

According to Kiyosaki, the government's inability to curb spending will lead to massive money printing in the future. This might erode the purchasing power of the U.S. dollar.

"The BIG PRINT is about to begin," Kiyosaki warned.

Recent findings suggest that this is the core reason for his investments in Bitcoin and Ethereum. He believes that these assets will rise in value when the government is forced to aggressively print money in response to escalating financial concerns.

It has been revealed that moreover, he believes that holding these crypto assets directly would be better than investing in exchange-traded funds (ETFs). However, he did not offer a reason for his opposition to ETFs in his post.

Furthermore, Kiyosaki stated that the next financial crisis could be much bigger than the global financial crisis of 2008.

"This crash we are just now sliding into is much bigger than 2008. Possibly a global depression," he commented.

He also mentioned that his gold, silver, Bitcoin and Ethereum holdings could make him one of the ultra-rich if his predictions come true.

In a recent development, however, Kiyosaki mentioned some figures that were not entirely accurate. For instance, he stated that the U.S. national debt stood at $49 trillion. But according to Treasury data, the national debt was about $40.7 trillion in November 2026. Also, his claim that the U.S. is printing $1 trillion every 90 days conflates government debt with money printing.

Although Kiyosaki is a strong believer in Bitcoin, he recently advised investors not to buy Bitcoin immediately amid the digital asset's current price slump.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 20, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author cautioned against catching a 'falling knife.'.

"Never grab a falling knife." This means that investors should wait for the market crash to end before buying.

"I started buying bitcoin around $20k after the market crashed last time," Kiyosaki recalled.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," he added.

The AI boom helped lift retirement accounts, but the Nvidia whiplash showed how much investors’ financial futures depend on a handful of stocks

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Millions of Americans, and their financial futures, may be exposed to the recent AI-fueled swings in the market regardless of whether they’ve ever used a chatbot.
  • Stocks plunged Wednesday morning before recovering much of the loss.
  • Sources indicate that wednesday’s swing capped a week in which a single tech giant’s board decision moved the index that holds much of Americans’ retirement accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Millions of Americans, and their financial futures, may be exposed to the recent AI-fueled swings in the market regardless of whether they’ve ever used a chatbot.

Stocks plunged Wednesday morning before recovering much of the loss. Near the start of trading, the Dow fell more than 1,000 points and the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% as AI chip stocks sold off for a second straight day. Nvidia fell as much as 8%. By late afternoon, the S&P 500 had cut its loss to about half a percent, and the Dow had turned higher.

Sources indicate that wednesday’s swing capped a week in which a single tech giant’s board decision moved the index that holds much of Americans’ retirement accounts. Roughly two-thirds of of Fidelity 401(k) savers keep everything in a target-date fund.

Following a tumultuous few weeks in which Jensen Huang resigned and was later reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker’s stock jumped 31%, added about $950 billion in market value, and lifted the S&P 500 by 4.7%. Still, the S&P 500 is now about 8% below its Oct. 6 record. Last Friday it closed 11.6% below that high, putting it in correction territory, after seven straight losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

Stock market concentration has been on the rise for years, and it is now near 35-year highs. Just 10 stocks in the S&P 500 account for about 39% of its total market capitalization, with the five largest stocks—all tech giants—alone accounting for 29%, according to Charles Schwab. That means an American with $100,000 in an index fund tied to the S&P 500 would have $29,000 in just five stocks.

As a result, many investors may think they are putting money into a diversified investment when the health of their portfolios may actually be tied more to the fate of a handful of tech giants than they realize, said Martin Mulyadi, a professor of accounting at Shenandoah University’s College of Business, Engineering & Technology.

“An index fund spreads your money across 500 companies, but it does not spread the risk evenly,” he told Fortune.

It has been revealed that for the millions of Americans who have poured their money into S&P 500 index funds through their 401(k)s, this concentration has been a boon in recent years. A booming stock market that has risen just over 50% during the past five years helped push the number of 401(k) millionaires at Fidelity to a record 769,000 in June. Even before the selloff began, that number had fallen some 2% between the second and third quarters, but was still up 15% from a year earlier, according to Fidelity.

In a recent development, through the third quarter, the vast majority of retirement savers were still investing. About 96% of 401(k) participants at Fidelity either maintained or increased their savings rate during the third quarter, the financial services company revealed in a report this week.

“Despite market volatility, many workers continue to increase their savings, stay invested, and take advantage of workplace retirement plan features designed to support long-term success,” Sharon Brovelli, Fidelity’s president of workplace investing, said in a statement.

Yet the growing dominance of a handful of technology giants means even those who have followed conventional retirement wisdom and have added to diversified funds may be exposed to heightened risk.

A further stock slide could hurt the portfolios of millions of Americans and especially for those closer to retirement: The average Fidelity 401(k) millionaire is 58 years old.

For older Americans, a downturn early in retirement could have implications for when they can afford to stop working and how much money they’ll have to live on once they do.

Recent findings suggest that by selling investments at depressed prices to cover living expenses, retirees face the problem of sequence-of-returns risk. If a falling stock market in early retirement causes retirees to sell their investments at lower prices, that means they have less money left in the market that could later benefit from an eventual recovery.

To try to avoid this phenomenon, Charles Schwab recommends maintaining a short-term reserve of low-risk and more liquid investments that retirees could draw from in a downturn to avoid touching their portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that the increasing concentration of the stock market also doesn’t necessarily mean investors should abandon index funds altogether. Investors should instead consider taking a closer look at the makeup of their portfolio, stated Sean McEvilly, the managing partner and founder of Vistamark Investments.

“The practical move isn’t to bail out of stocks. It’s to look at the whole 401(k), since target-date and large-cap funds often hold the same names, and make sure there’s real exposure to small and midsized companies, international stocks, and bonds,” McEvilly told Fortune.
